analysis.one_liner: Creates free digital bank accounts at the Federal Reserve for every American, with no fees.
analysis.headline: The bill to create free, no-fee Federal Reserve bank accounts was introduced in March 2020, drew zero cosponsors, got one committee hearing, and died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required Federal Reserve member banks to offer free "FedAccount" digital wallets to anyone who wanted one, with no fees, no minimum balance, and a basic interest rate. The accounts would have given millions of unbanked Americans a safe place to keep money and a direct way to receive COVID-19 stimulus payments. In areas with few bank branches, post offices would have served as the access point, and the Federal Reserve would have reimbursed post offices and small banks for their costs.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 7 million U.S. households without a bank account, and millions more who rely on costly check-cashers, prepaid cards, and overdraft fees, would have gained a free, safe account with a debit card, online access, and bill pay. Anyone waiting on a government payment — especially COVID-19 stimulus checks — could have received it instantly in a FedAccount instead of by slow paper check or high-fee prepaid card. Post offices and small banks and credit unions would have been paid by the Federal Reserve for the costs of offering the accounts, giving post offices a new source of revenue and small lenders direct access to Federal Reserve master accounts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unbanked and low-income households; post offices

how_it_helps.text: Every resident and citizen could open a free digital dollar wallet with no fees, no minimum balance, no maximum balance, and interest set at the Federal Reserve's reserve rate — services that commercial checking accounts typically charge for.

Member banks would have been required to open these wallets for anyone electing one, including people eligible for COVID-19 payments, so federal aid could land directly in an account instead of going out by delayed paper checks.

The accounts had to match the banks' existing services — debit cards, ATMs, online access, bill pay, mobile banking — and banks could not close an account for being unprofitable, protecting low-balance customers banks often shed.

In areas with limited bank access, including low- and moderate-income communities, post offices would have provided application and account services, with ATMs at postal facilities — putting a banking access point in thousands of neighborhoods that lack branches.

Post offices and banks under $10 billion in assets would have been reimbursed by the Federal Reserve for their costs, and state nonmember banks and credit unions could open Federal Reserve master accounts to offer the wallets themselves.

analysis.who_pays: Large member banks would have borne the direct cost: they would have had to set up and maintain the accounts, forgo all account fees on them, pay interest, and could not charge overdraft fees on them — losing fee income and risking deposits moving out of profitable products. The Federal Reserve would have reimbursed post offices and small banks for operating costs; because the Fed returns its earnings to the Treasury, that cost would ultimately fall on taxpayers in a small way. Banks over $10 billion in assets would have gotten no reimbursement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large banks, through lost fees and deposits

drawbacks.text: The wallets would pay interest at only the Federal Reserve's reserve rate, not market rates, and would offer no overdraft coverage — so as a primary account they would earn less than a good commercial account and provide no cushion for a short month; the design is aimed at people priced out of banking, not at replacing it for everyone.

If deposits moved heavily into FedAccounts, banks would have fewer funds to lend out, which bankers warned could shrink consumer credit — a real trade-off of routing money through the central bank rather than commercial lenders.

Putting so many accounts at the Federal Reserve and the Postal Service creates a single large target for cyberattack and a new operational mission for institutions with no retail banking experience, even though the bill does impose Bank Secrecy Act and tax-return-level privacy protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households who today pay check-cashing fees and overdraft charges for lack of a bank account, the benefit is concrete and immediate: a free account, a debit card, and a direct channel for government payments. The costs fall mostly on large banks, which would lose fee revenue and some deposits — a transfer from an industry's profits to consumers, not from the public. The real trade-offs are design ones: below-market interest and no overdraft coverage make the accounts a floor rather than a full banking replacement, and a government-run account system carries cybersecurity and implementation risk. On balance this was a targeted help-the-unbanked bill, and its failure means those households kept paying the fees it would have eliminated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced during the first COVID wave, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, got a single hearing in June 2020, and the committee never took it up again — it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on March 23, 2020, three days after Congress passed the CARES Act, as a way to get stimulus money directly and instantly into people's hands.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where it sat with no cosponsors joining from either party.
The committee held a hearing on June 30, 2020 — the only action the bill ever received after referral — but never scheduled a markup or a vote.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died in committee, as happens to the large majority of bills.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks came out ahead: the fee and deposit base the FedAccounts would have drawn from stayed intact, and the banking system was not asked to offer free public accounts. Unbanked households, post offices, and small banks gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks, which kept fee income and deposits

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH), Ranking Member, Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as its sole sponsor during the COVID-19 payment rollout and pressed for it in the Banking Committee, which held a June 2020 hearing where it was discussed.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Allowed one hearing but never scheduled a markup or committee vote, leaving the bill to die in committee at the end of the Congress.

against.name: American Bankers Association and commercial banking industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed the FedAccount public banking option, arguing it would pull deposits and fee revenue out of commercial banks.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and it died in a Republican-run committee after one hearing.

industries.note: Member banks over $10 billion in assets would have had to offer the wallets free of charge, absorb the operating costs, and give up fee income on accounts that could not be closed for being unprofitable. Their gain from the bill's death was keeping the current fee-based checking system intact.

industries.industry: Check cashers, payday lenders, and prepaid card providers
industries.note: These businesses earn their revenue from people without bank accounts — check-cashing fees, high-cost small loans, and fee-laden prepaid cards used to receive government payments. Free FedAccounts would have removed much of their customer base.

Post offices would have become the banking access point in underserved areas and been reimbursed by the Federal Reserve for their costs, adding revenue and a public-facing service role for a financially strained agency.

They would have gained Federal Reserve master account access and cost reimbursement for offering the wallets — tools they currently lack — but would also have competed against a free direct option from the Fed itself.
